content: The use of specific antimalarial drugs is likely to influence the cost-effectiveness of Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (SMC). Further details on this topic can be found in the summary of contextual factors report for SMC by Bhattarai et al. (unpublished evidence). The Guideline Development Group (GDG) considered that SMC is likely to enhance equitable service delivery, as evidenced by similar intervention coverage across wealth quintiles in all countries where it is implemented (Bhattarai et al., unpublished evidence). There were no significant differences in SMC coverage by age or gender. The recommendation for SMC was developed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. The World Health Organization (WHO) commissioned a systematic review to inform this guidance on SMC (Thwing et al., unpublished evidence). Additionally, a separate report summarized evidence from published studies on contextual factors related to SMC implementation, including cost-effectiveness, feasibility, equity, values, and acceptability (Bhattarai et al., unpublished evidence). This information was supplemented by a cross-cutting review on chemoprevention drug resistance (Plowe, unpublished evidence), a civil society consultation report on chemoprevention (CS4ME, unpublished evidence), and contributions from GDG members, including representatives from national malaria programs. The systematic review aimed to assess the impact of SMC with antimalarial drugs on malaria disease burden among children in areas with seasonal malaria transmission. It focused on specific factors such as the age of children (3–59 months vs. 60–120 months), the number of treatment cycles during a season (3–4 cycles vs. 5–6 cycles), and the drug regimen. It also summarized contextual information regarding acceptability, feasibility, equity, safety, drug resistance, cost, and cost-effectiveness. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of confirmed clinical malaria. Other outcomes included parasite prevalence, incidence of infection, anemia prevalence, blood transfusions, hospital admissions, severe malaria, all-cause mortality, adverse reactions, and school attendance. Seventeen studies met the inclusion criteria for the review, including 12 randomized and five non-randomized studies. All studies were conducted in sub-Saharan Africa, specifically in Burkina Faso, Gambia, Ghana, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, and Senegal. Twelve studies used sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine plus amodiaquine (SP+AQ), three used artesunate-amodiaquine (AS-AQ), one used SP+artesunate (SP+AS), and one used artemether-lumefantrine (AL). Trials administering three to four cycles were typically conducted in areas with shorter transmission seasons, while those administering five to six cycles were in areas with longer transmission seasons. None of the included studies reported the incidence of infection or blood transfusions as outcome measures. One study reported educational outcomes but did not include school attendance. The GDG appraised evidence from the systematic review and supporting information in October 2021. They concluded that SMC has a significant beneficial effect, with the balance of desirable and undesirable effects favoring SMC. The costs of implementing SMC are moderate, though the overall cost is influenced by the drug used and the delivery method. SMC is cost-effective, but expanding it to age groups beyond those at the highest risk of severe disease or to areas with lower malaria transmission, as well as using more expensive antimalarials, could reduce its cost-effectiveness. SMC was deemed acceptable, with refusal rates below 1% in five countries (Bhattarai et al., unpublished evidence). Consequently, the GDG considered SMC acceptable to key stakeholders. SMC delivery approaches and coverage vary across countries. For example, in Gambia, delivery through village health workers achieved substantially higher coverage than delivery by reproductive and child health teams (74% vs. 48%, a difference of 27%; 95% CI: 16%–38%). Overall, the GDG judged SMC implementation to be feasible. The GDG strongly recommended SMC for age groups at high risk of severe malaria living in areas of seasonal malaria transmission to reduce disease burden. The effect of introducing SMC can be evaluated using routine hospital, clinic, or community health worker data. The WHO chemoprevention efficacy study (CPES) protocol should be used to monitor the efficacy of medicines used for chemoprevention. While the potential effect of chemoprevention on the spread of drug resistance can be monitored through molecular marker analysis, the correlation between these markers and the efficacy of antimalarials for chemoprevention remains unclear and should be interpreted cautiously. The GDG identified several evidence gaps requiring further research, including the operational effectiveness of SMC, the value of administering SMC to children aged 10 years or older, the effectiveness of SMC in areas with seasonal but prolonged malaria transmission, the effectiveness of SMC in areas with antimalarial drug resistance, better understanding of the pharmacokinetics of drugs used for chemoprevention, and the efficacy of delivering SMC with alternative drug combinations and intervals between cycles. Intermittent preventive treatment in school-aged children (IPTsc) involves administering a full treatment course of antimalarial medicine at regular intervals to treat and prevent malaria infections in children old enough to attend school. IPTsc has been evaluated in children aged 5–15 years, though the burden of malaria and benefits of IPTsc may vary across this age range. Evidence is limited. National malaria programs may consider IPTsc if resources allow its introduction among school-aged children without compromising chemoprevention for those at the highest risk of severe disease, such as children under 5 years old. Schools may provide a low-cost means to deliver chemoprevention to school-aged children, but seasonal variation in malaria transmission and school term timing may necessitate alternative delivery channels to maximize impact. Firstand second-line malaria treatments should not be used for IPTsc if safe and effective alternatives are available. The dosing schedule for IPTsc should be informed by local malaria epidemiology and timed to provide protection during periods of greatest malaria risk. Most trials provided IPTsc monthly or each school term. In settings with perennial transmission, higher transmission intensity may increase the value of drugs with longer half-lives or more frequent dosing. If IPTsc cannot be maintained year-round in perennial transmission settings due to resource constraints, it may be timed to provide protection during transmission peaks. IPTsc can be delivered through schools or community-based approaches. The delivery method should consider local malaria epidemiology and whether school-based delivery aligns with peak malaria transmission. Special efforts may be needed to target children not attending school, as they are likely at higher risk of malaria. Communication with communities, teachers, caregivers, and children is essential to maximize understanding and acceptability among key stakeholders. The impact of drug resistance on the protection provided by IPTsc is currently unclear. A re-analysis of data on resistance markers following monthly IPTsc found no evidence of increased prevalence of resistance markers after DHA-P administration. However, expanded use of antimalarial medicines may increase resistance and eventually undermine efficacy. Using different drugs for chemoprevention and treatment, and combining drugs with counteracting resistance mechanisms, may help preserve efficacy. Children with sickle cell disease should be included in IPTsc unless they already receive regular chemoprevention for their condition. Co-delivery of IPTsc alongside other school health programs should consider drug manufacturers’ guidance regarding potential interactions.
